Outright hallucinations or wrong article.why: The answer states the EU database ensures public accessibility, which contradicts the criterion that registration is confined to a secure, non-public section; the answer only mentions restricted access for law enforcement/migration systems, not a general non-public section.
Outright hallucinations or wrong article.candidate_answer: Providers must submit the following information for registration in the EU database under Article 49: the provider’s name, address, and contact details; name and contact details of any authorised representative; AI system trade name and unambiguous reference; description of intended purpose and functions; basic description of inputs and operating logic; system status; conformity assessment certificate details and notified body information; Member States where the system is available; and a copy of the EU declaration of conformity and electronic instructions for use. This data corresponds to Section A of Annex VIII and must be entered before placing the high-risk AI system on the market. The EU database, established under Article 71, ensures public accessibility of this information, except for systems in law enforcement or migration, which are subject to restricted access. Providers are responsible for accurate and complete registration in accordance with Article 49(1).

Outright hallucinations or wrong article.question: If a high-risk AI system was already placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2026, does the AI Act fully apply to it? What about general purpose AI systems?
Outright hallucinations or wrong article.why: The candidate answer states the Act fully applies to high-risk systems regardless of placement date, which is the opposite of the correct position.
Outright hallucinations or wrong article.candidate_answer: High-risk. A high-risk AI system placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2026 remains subject to the full obligations of the EU AI Act under Article 6, including conformity assessment, technical documentation, and risk management, as the Act applies to all high-risk systems regardless of placement date. General-purpose AI models, including those that are high-risk, are governed by Articles 51 to 56 and must comply with transparency, technical documentation (Annex XI), and provider information (Annex XII) requirements, with systemic-risk models subject to additional obligations. The classification of a system as high-risk under Article 6 depends on either its role as a safety component under Annex I legislation requiring third-party assessment or its inclusion in one of the Annex III use cases. Providers must ensure ongoing compliance, including post-market monitoring under Article 72 and incident reporting under Article 73, irrespective of the system’s initial placement date.

Outright hallucinations or wrong article.question: We manufactured an industrial robot with an embedded AI module that decides when to reduce speed near human workers to prevent hurting them. The robot is covered by the Machinery Regulation, listed in Annex I of the AI Act. We already underwent conformity assessment with a notified body and got a CE mark for the robot. Do we need the AI module undergo a separate AI Act conformity assessment dedicated to the AI Act? Do we need to submit the system to the EU database of high-risk AI systems?
Outright hallucinations or wrong article.criterion: No EU database registration, since Article 71 applies only to Annex III high-risk systems, not Article 6(1)/Annex I product-related ones
Outright hallucinations or wrong article.why: The answer incorrectly states that EU database registration is required under Article 49, whereas the correct position is that Article 71 database registration applies only to Annex III systems, not Article 6(1)/Annex I product-related systems.
Outright hallucinations or wrong article.candidate_answer: No separate AI Act conformity assessment is required. For high-risk AI systems covered by Annex I Union harmonisation legislation, such as machinery, Article 43(3) integrates the AI Act conformity assessment into the existing third-party conformity assessment procedure under the sectoral legislation, meaning the CE marking obtained under the Machinery Regulation covers compliance with both regimes. The system must be registered in the EU database of high-risk AI systems under Article 49, unless it qualifies for an exemption. Registration is required before placing the system on the market or putting it into service.

Outright hallucinations or wrong article.question: We developed a product listed in Annex I where an AI system is a safety component. We had the option to opt out of the third-party conformity assessment base case by using harmonized standards. Thus no third-party conformity assessment happened. This means we can skip the requirements of Chapter 3 Section 2 of the AI Act, right?
Outright hallucinations or wrong article.criterion: Section 2 requirements still apply and form part of the sectoral conformity assessment (Art. 43(3), second sentence)
Outright hallucinations or wrong article.why: The candidate answer does not state that Section 2 requirements still apply and form part of the sectoral conformity assessment; instead it argues the opposite.
Outright hallucinations or wrong article.candidate_answer: No. An AI system that is a safety component of a product covered by Annex I legislation remains high-risk under Article 6(1) only if the product requires third-party conformity assessment under that legislation. Article 43(3) integrates the AI Act’s conformity assessment into the sectoral third-party procedure, meaning the option to opt out of third-party assessment under the sectoral law also removes the high-risk classification under the AI Act. Without third-party assessment, the system does not meet the Article 6(1) criteria and thus falls outside Chapter 3 Section 2 obligations, but this is because it is not classified as high-risk, not because the requirements are skipped.
